title: Efficacy of osimertinib for lung squamous cell carcinoma with de novo EGFR T790M-positive: Case report and literature review.
abstract: Among epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancers, squamous cell carcinoma is less common and shows lower responsiveness to first-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) compared to adenocarcinoma.
However, the efficacy of osimertinib for squamous cell carcinoma with EGFR mutations is not well known.
This study reports the case of a 57-year-old male diagnosed as having stage IIIC squamous cell lung cancer.
Oncomine Dx Target Test identified EGFR exon19 deletion and de novo EGFR T790M mutation with variant allele frequencies (VAF) of 21.6% and 25.2%, respectively.
The patient was treated with osimertinib after progression on chemoradiotherapy followed by durvalumab, and a partial response was maintained for more than 20 months.
To predict EGFR-TKI efficacy, confirmation of gene mutations and VAF using next-generation sequencing is helpful.

body.text: Most epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) are adenocarcinomas, while squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) are relatively rare.

Previous clinical trials have reported that first- to third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR mutation-positive lung adenocarcinomas (LAD) but their effectiveness is lower in SCC.
The acquisition of the EGFR T790M mutation in exon20 is the most common molecular mechanism leading to resistance to first- or second-generation EGFR-TKI in EGFR mutation-positive NSCLC.
However, the third-generation EGFR-TKI, osimertinib, has shown high efficacy against this resistant mutation.
Primary EGFR T790M mutation detected at diagnosis (known as de novo EGFR T790M mutation) is often detected simultaneously with EGFR-TKI-sensitive EGFR mutations.
Here, we report the case of a patient with SCC having both an EGFR exon 19 deletion and a de novo T790M mutation, who exhibited a positive response to treatment with osimertinib.
The patient was a 57-year-old male with no significant medical or smoking history.
He visited the hospital complaining of right chest pain and dyspnea.
Computed tomography (CT) revealed an 11 cm mass located in the upper lobe of the right lung (Figure 1).
The tumor markers squamous cell carcinoma antigen (17.3 ng/mL) was elevated.
On the other hand, carcinoembryonic antigen was in the normal range (1.3 ng/mL).
A CT-guided biopsy was performed on the primary tumor.
Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed polygonal cells with intercellular bridges, p40 positive, thyroid transcription factor-1 negative, which were seen throughout the specimen.
The diagnosis was squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), clinical stage T4N3M0 (Figure 2).
EGFR exon19 deletion and de novo EGFR T790M mutation were detected using the Oncomine Dx Target Test, with variant allele frequency (VAF) of 21.6% and 25.2%, respectively.

The other mutation was not found by Oncomine Comprehensive Assay (OCA version 3; Thermo Fisher Scientific) which was performed in the lung cancer genomic screening project for individualized medicine in Japan (LC-SCRUM) (UMIN ID: UMIN000010234).

After chemoradiotherapy followed by one course of durvalumab consolidation therapy, a single brain metastasis appeared; therefore, durvalumab was terminated, and stereotactic radiotherapy was performed.
Approximately 4 months after the last administration of durvalumab, the primary tumor had increased in size and was evaluated as progressive disease (PD).
At the time of diagnosis, EGFR exon19 deletion and de novo EGFR T790M mutation were detected, and osimertinib was initiated.
Two months later, a partial response (PR) was achieved, and the tumor maintained shrinkage for more than 20 months (Figure 3).

Although osimertinib was administered after treatment with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), the patient was able to continue treatment without any adverse events such as drug-induced lung injury.

To the best of our knowledge, a literature search for case reports of osimertinib in SCC patients with EGFR mutation-positive tumors, yielded 16 cases, including the present case, , , , , , , , , , , , (Table 1).
The treatment outcome breakdown was 12 cases of PR and four cases of PD, and many were reported to be effective, but the duration of response was limited in some cases.

On the other hand, previous reports of first-generation EGFR-TKI in EGFR mutation-positive SCC showed ORR of 25.0%-43.2%, OS of 13.48-18.04 months, and PFS of 1.4-5.6 months,, , , which was a poor outcome compared to the therapeutic effects to LAD.
The reasons for the difference in response between LAD and SCC remain unclear.
However, it has been reported that the response to EGFR-TKIs, including osimertinib, is associated with VAF and the presence of coexisting gene abnormalities.
This trend was also observed in this case study.

Balazs et al. reported that EGFR-TKI significantly prolonged PFS and OS in the group with adjusted tumoral EGFR variant allele frequency (EGFR-aVAF) ≥70%, which is VAF divided by the estimated percentage of neoplastic cells, compared with the group with EGFR-aVAF <70%.

In the present case, the percentage of neoplastic cells was 30%, and the aVAFs of EGFR exon19 deletion and EGFR T790M mutation were 72% and 84%, respectively; therefore, a certain level of efficacy was expected.

Regarding coexisting gene abnormalities, previous reports suggest that such as EGFR C797X mutation, MET amplification, alterations in the RAS-RAF-MAPK pathway, and ROS-1 fusion gene are associated with resistance to osimertinib., In fact, in a previous report by Nishimura et al., in which osimertinib was administered as first-line chemotherapy to a SCC patient who was EGFR exon19 deletion-positive, but was completely ineffective, genetic abnormalities such as TP53, CDK6, and KRAS were found simultaneously.
In this case, no coexisting genetic abnormalities were detected, which may have been associated with a good response to the treatment.
In conclusion, it is essential to actively search for driver gene, even in cases of SCC.
This is because cases exhibiting driver gene mutations with a response to molecular-targeted drugs have been documented.
In addition, the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs may be affected by VAF and the presence of coexisting gene abnormalities.
Therefore, it is important to perform next-generation sequencing to predict the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs.
